home.title: Homes Without Divisions | Legal resources for subdivided unit tenants

hero.eyebrow: A Pro Bono HK community legal empowerment initiative
hero.lead: Free legal resources for tenants in Hong Kong subdivided units. Working with tenants, frontline workers and landlords, we turn protection on paper into something you can actually use.

deliverables.heading: Three documents, for the three moments that decide a tenancy
deliverables.lead: Each one answers a different part of what makes a tenancy equitable. All free to download, reproduce and share.

pillars.heading: What makes a tenancy equitable?
pillars.lead: We break it into three concrete things. The three resources exist so that each of them is actually achievable.

notice.heading: This is legal information, not legal advice
notice.lead: This site and its resources give general legal information. They cannot take account of the facts of your own tenancy. If any of the following is happening, stop and speak to a social worker, a lawyer or the police straight away:
items: You have been given a notice to quit, a demand for possession, or any court document.
The locks have been changed, your belongings have been removed, or you are being kept out of your home.
Water or electricity has been cut off, or a shared facility blocked, to make you leave.
You are being threatened, intimidated or harassed.
There is a fire safety, structural or electrical danger in the unit or the building.
You repeatedly cannot pay rent, or you have nowhere to go if the tenancy ends.
notice.footnote: Harassment of a tenant with intent to make the tenant give up the unit is a criminal offence under section 120AAZO of the Landlord and Tenant (Consolidation) Ordinance (Cap. 7).

hero.heading: Turning protection on paper into the capacity to act
hero.lead: Homes Without Divisions is a community legal empowerment initiative by Pro Bono HK for tenants living in subdivided units. Our mission is to advance the next generation of equitable tenancy in Hong Kong.

mission.heading: Adequate housing is a right, not a matter of luck
body: Article 39 of the Basic Law keeps the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in force in Hong Kong. Article 11(1) of the Covenant recognises the universal right to adequate housing. Under the Special Rapporteur's guidelines, that right covers security of tenure, availability of services, affordability, habitability, accessibility, appropriate location and cultural adequacy.

Living in a subdivided unit should not mean giving any of that up. With the Basic Housing Units reform now changing both tenancy control and housing standards, it matters more than ever that tenants know where they stand.

methods.name: Standard-setting
methods.body: Publishing a model tenancy agreement and supporting documents that any tenant and landlord can adopt, so both sides start from the same terms and the same understanding.

methods.name: Capacity-building
methods.body: Explaining what the law already gives you and how to use it in practice — not only knowing, but being able to act.

pillars.heading: The three parts of an equitable tenancy
pillars.lead: They hold each other up. Take any one away and the other two get weaker. Choose one below to see what it means.
pillars.diagramDescription: Three overlapping circles representing transparent communication, fair terms and conduct, and appropriate solution. Where all three overlap is a human-oriented equitable tenancy. Two dotted circles around the outside mark our two ways of working: standard-setting and capacity-building.

capability.heading: From having a right to being able to use it
body: The Without Divisions ethos is grounded in a humanist view of law, inspired by the capability approach to human welfare developed by Amartya Sen and others. We notice how, despite formal legal protections, it is often difficult to translate them across the fabric of society into meaningful empowerment.

The capability approach emphasises the freedom to achieve through human agency. It reminds us that what is right or good does not simply arrive with a list of rights, nor because that is how things have always worked. It is about how we, with help from the community, build the opportunity and the capacity to live a better life.

For tenants in subdivided units, that means more than having statutory protections on paper. It means being able to understand your tenancy, communicate on fair terms, seek solutions without fear, and exercise real agency in the everyday decisions a tenancy demands.

Whoever you are reading this — a tenant, a frontline NGO worker, someone about to move into a subdivided unit, or simply a curious member of the public — we hope these resources point you in the right direction the next time you have a choice to make.

schedule-of-condition.name: Schedule of Condition
schedule-of-condition.summary: Record the real condition of the unit, the shared facilities and the key tenancy facts, item by item, so both sides start from the same set of facts.
points: Log the condition of every fitting and appliance, and raise anything missing or broken at once
Confirm how the common areas may be used
Ask whether the flat has Basic Housing Unit recognition or grace-period registration

model-tenancy-agreement.name: Model Tenancy Agreement
model-tenancy-agreement.summary: A lawyer-checked, party-neutral tenancy agreement in plain language that reflects what the law actually requires, and adds nothing extra to either side's burden.
points: Avoids the invalid and unlawful terms common in off-the-shelf templates
Plain language without losing legal accuracy
Optional addenda covering pets, landlord's agents and more

pocket-tenancy-clinic.name: Pocket Tenancy Clinic
pocket-tenancy-clinic.nameSecondary: 分間單位租務解難手冊
pocket-tenancy-clinic.summary: A clinic you can carry. Work through the diagnostics form to see where you stand, then go to the Treatment Room your answers point to — each with concrete steps to take.
points: Tenancy Risk Diagnostics Form: three parts, 36 statements
Ten Treatment Rooms for the ten most common tenancy problems
Two Emergency Rooms, for a tenant's death and for anyone claiming to act for your landlord
